To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1‐Napthyl‐β-D‐glucuronidase, a metabolite of 1‐nathol, was injected into the rat brain.
the efflux of 1‐nphthyl‐βD‐glucurinide from the brain is mediated by both diffusion and efflux transport processes.
the elimination from brain of an intracerebraly formed xenobiotic metabolite, 1-naphthyl-beta-D-glucuronide, is a combination of diffusion and an efflux process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of a brain‐specific isoform of UDP‐gluconyltransferase and its in vivo elimination.
the study of a new brain‐specific isoform of UDP‐gluronyltransferases and the efflux mechanism of a metabolite formed in situ in the rat brain.
the in vivo characterization of the efflux process of a hydrosolubile compound, which is formed by a brain isoform of UDP‐glucuronyltransferase.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elimination from the brain of intracerebraly formed glucuronides is due to the combination of diffusion and active transport.
the elimination of the brain‐derived metabolite 1N‐β‐Dglucuronide is a complex phenomenon, involving both diffusion and a carrier‐mediated transport process.
1‐n aphthyl‐β ‐D‐glucur onide is eliminated from the rat brain by both passive diffusion and an active efflux mechanism, the latter being saturable and of low capacity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the elimination of the glucuronide formed from the xenobiotic 1‐nphthol is not only dependent on the diffusion of the molecule through the blood–brain barriers but also on the activity of the specific transport systems present in the endothelial cells of the cerebral microcirculation.
1‐NAG is formed in the brain by a saturable process and is cleared from brain by a saturate process.

1‐n aphthyl‐βD‐glucuroni de is a good model compound to study the elimination of a polar metabolite from the brain tissue, and it could also be used to evaluate the potential of the efflux pump P‐gp to eliminate a glucuronide.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the brain, glucuronide formation can be an important route for the elimination of xenobiotics and their metabolites.
the brain is capable of eliminating xenobiotic metabolites, which is an important consideration in the context of drug development.
, as the brain is not a homogeneous tissue, the clearance of an intracerebrically formed glucuronide from different brain regions is not identical and depends on its regional concentration.
